utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer, Lisa Biersay, Thomas Laugel and intern, August Sommerfeld, appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and Ms. Liane Aronchick, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would remind you that you are still under oath. Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you comfortable where you are?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to continue from our discussion yesterday, and I'd like to ask you about what medical supplies you had access to while you were in the Stajicevo detention camp.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my own medical bag. My two paramedics also had two satchels with drugs which I had selected while I was in the shelter in the Borovo factory. When we were told that we would be let go to Vinkovci, that's the drugs that I took and those were the only drugs that we had in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Regarding Vinkovci, you said that you were told that you would be going to Vinkovci. When you were told that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night before the surrender. We were told that it had been agreed that the children, the women, and the seriously sick and injured would be allowed to go to Vinkovci; whereas the remainder of the people would be detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were in the Stajicevo camp, did you ask for additional supplies from the commanders of the camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day -- or, rather, every morning Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic asked me if I needed something, and I told him yes. I made a list. I gave it to him. And I waited for a couple of days, three days. Every day he asked the same thing, every day I gave him a list. The third day I asked him when the drugs would be forthcoming, and he said it wasn't easy because he was handing the list over the Serbian Red Cross. The Serbian Red Cross, in its turn, would give it to the International Red Cross and waiting for a donation, and then when that donation arrived we would be provided with drugs. And the chain would be the same. The International Red Cross would give it to the Serbian Red Cross and then the Serbian Red Cross would give it to the camp. The procedure was the same in the detention camp. Every day I was asked the same question, every day my answer was the same, and nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "every day my answer was the same," did you mean the answer that you received was the same?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The answer was that we would be provided with drugs when they were provided to the Serbian cross from the International Red Cross, and nothing came out of it. We never received anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who is Ivan Kunac?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a detainee. Unfortunately, he died in the camp as a result of the interrogation. He was beaten until he fainted, and then in the evening they brought him back to the camp after having been interrogated, and the following morning we were told that he got seriously ill, and then Dr. Nadas went to examine him, and then he called Dr. Emedi, who was a specialist. He was all covered in blood. And then they asked the lieutenant-colonel to send him to a hospital, and then the lieutenant-colonel said that a medical doctor would come to examine him. This same afternoon a doctor came who introduced herself as a medical [as interpreted] doctor, she examined him, and she said that he did not need medical -- hospital treatment because he would recover. And she said that she would return the following day to re-examine him. He died during the night. She returned the following evening and she thought that he was dead, and her comment was, I did not think that he was in such a bad condition. I'm really surprised to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was in the evening after he had been interrogated that --

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we didn't know how bad he was. They just left him there. Nobody knew. The remainder of the detainees were asleep.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The lady who came to examine was a "military doctor," not a "medical doctor."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, at what times of the day would you see prisoners who had been injured during interrogations?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly in the evening after interrogations. When they returned, they sought my attention, and I attended to them and I helped them as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could injured prisoners walk up to you freely and ask for medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A guard would come to fetch us and escort us to the injured person or, alternatively, that injured people would be brought to us. We were not allowed to walk freely around the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Turning now to tab 36, which is annotated 65 ter number 2410.2. If possible, I'd like to give a hard copy of the document to the witness because it contains some colouring on it and it takes a while for it to load in e-court. Thank you. If we could turn to the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Dr. Malla, directing your attention to the document you have before you, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names of those people who were detained in Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you go through this 23-page document and highlight the names of those people you recognise as being at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see my signature there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you signed each page of this document?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed every page and I put a date on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd ask for the admission of 65 ter number 2410.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1516, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Regarding the highlights that you made, Dr. Malla, these names, are there -- do you know if these people are Serbs or non-Serbs, the ones that you've highlighted?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among them there are people who are of Serb ethnicity and those who are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how many Serb names you highlighted?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps three or four, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the other names, were they all non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Muslims, Croats, Hungarians, Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to page 9 to the name Jeftic that's highlighted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, before we go into the details, could you ask the witness, please, how many in total are highlighted so that we have an idea of proportions between Serbs and non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, do you recall how many names total you highlighted in the document, or would you need time to count them?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not count them initially, so if you want me to count them, that's the only way I can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: An approximate figure, Dr. Malla? Because we don't have the document in front of us. We just have one page. So do we have ten highlighted names or a hundred? I mean, it's 23 pages long.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Turning to page 1. Let's go to page 1, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And looking at those names, would you agree that there are five names highlighted on that page?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the next page?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the next page?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the next?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on page 5?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three. Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on page 6?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 7?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on page 8?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on page 9?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And staying on page 9, the very first highlight, the name Jeftic, what is the ethnicity or nationality of that person?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on page 10?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Page 11?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And directing your attention, if we could stay on page 11 for a minute, do you recognise the name of a Serb person on that page?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And whose name is that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Nenad Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And page 12?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is your name on that page?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And page 13?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 14?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 15?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we move from that, the name Nadas on that page - you mentioned the name Nadas several times during your testimony - is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Dr. Radislav Nadas, who was a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 16?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 17?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 18?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 19?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The name Turkalj on page 21?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was that person ever injured at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was shot at. We could not treat him. We couldn't treat his wounds, so he was taken to hospital. Three days later we asked after him and we were told that unfortunately he had died. When I was leaving the camp during the second exchange of the detainees, a detainee from Mitrovica told me that person is alive. He's still in the camp. And as for us who were in Stajicevo, they lied to us that he had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 22, Dr. Malla?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And finally on page 23?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Malla, when did the International Red Cross come to the Stajicevo camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how long had you been in the camp by that point?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the days before the Red Cross came to the camp, did you notice any changes in the conditions of the camp?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, three days earlier, around the 7th December, was the first time when a water tap was installed in the camp. And on the tenth or the eleventh day, we heard that something was happening outside the barn and we learned that they had put up a fence and that they had installed a field toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, unless --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it about the date, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's about the timing --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Three days before and then the 7 December.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, you said that the International Red Cross came on the 2nd of December, and in the translation that we have it says that three days before on the 7th of December the changes started happening.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Water arrived and nothing else. And then -- and then on either the tenth or the eleventh there was some works going on. We didn't know what was going on. We were not allowed to even peek. And then later we learned that they had put up a fence and that they had installed a latrine in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla when did -- I apologise for interrupting, I'm still trying to work on the approximate dates that these events happened. You said that the Red Cross came on the 2nd of December; right? So December 2. And you said the changes started before. But the dates that you're giving us, the 10th and the 11th, they're after the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, that was on the tenth or eleventh day our stay in the camp. That's how I'm counting the days. On the seventh day of our stay in the camp at the request of us, doctors who work there, who dressed people's wounds, who administered therapies, we had not washed our hands for seven days because there was no water. There was just provisions to have a glass of water, but no water to wash. So at our request, the lieutenant-colonel installed a water facility on the seventh day of our stay, and that was the first time I could wash my hands. On the 30th of November work started outdoors there. We only heard that. And then somebody opened the door and said the Red Cross was coming and they allowed us to go out. And that was the first time that we were allowed to go out. That was the first time we saw the latrine and that was the first time we could walk a bit, and that was the first time when we had a hot meal. The first time ever since we had been brought to the camp. And those changes were introduced only for the sake of the Red Cross. If they had not arrived, maybe we would have continued relieving ourselves by the wall. Maybe we would have been eating cold and meager meals for a number of days to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Malla, could you please - and it's just a last clarification - could you please focus on the dates and the days, not go into what exactly -- what happened. But in the record now it is said -- your testimony is that on the 2nd of December the Red Cross arrived, and then three days earlier - that is three days before the 2nd - and then the record says, and that's what I want to have right, around the 7th December. And with your explanation, I now understand that you meant to say around the seventh day we were in the camp. That's the day that you got a water tap installed; right? So we have 2nd of December, three days before, and three days before is the seventh day of your stay in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not correct. I was in the camp for 12 days. On the seventh day of my stay we got water, and on the ninth day of my stay the works started outside, on the ninth, tenth, and eleventh day of my stay. And then on the twelfth day of my stay, the Red Cross arrived. And on day nine, ten, eleven, we only heard that things were happening outside, and we didn't know what that was until the day we were allowed to go out and then we realised that a fence had been put up, that there was a latrine, and that's when we realised what the racket was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think now the time-line is clear, Dr. Malla. Thank you very much. Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described the latrine being built in the few days before the Red Cross came. Was there ever a time before the Red Cross came when a prisoner complained about having to relieve himself inside the barn itself?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all needed that from the first day, me too. We all complained because we were relieving ourselves in the same place where we were eating and sitting and everything, and it's really a stroke of luck that in those ten days there were no outbreaks of diseases.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did anyone ask to be able to go outside to relieve himself?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think on the third day of our arrival there, a man gathered his courage and he asked the guard, he told him that he had to relieve himself, and then this guard asks someone, I don't know, a superior of his, a military superior, what to do, and then they let him go out but he was escorted by three guards and he was taken outside into the dark. While he was relieving himself, there were these three standing there with their automatic rifles pointed at him. And then when he was done they started abusing him verbally and beating him, and finally he did not manage to relieve himself all the way. And then when he returned, when they took him back, no one thought of asking to be taken outside to be allowed to relieve himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described to the Trial Chamber just now about the quality of the food you had in the camp before the Red Cross came. Could you give the Trial Chamber an idea of how much you had to eat each day before the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th we were captured and that whole day until the evening, including the evening, we didn't get anything. On the 20th in the morning, Dr. Emedi and I asked the colonel to provide us some food because there were among the detainees some 20 or so men who were diabetics, and the colonel asked some -- around 14 loaves of bread and some lettuce. So these diabetics ate and we did too. Now, the second day no one got any food. The third day, we each received a piece of bread and a triangle, a piece of cheese. It's a small piece of cheese. There would be six of those triangles in a box. Now, on the second or third day of our stay in the camp, we received in the evening a piece of bread, a hotdog that would be divided into three pieces so that each detainee would only get a third of that hotdog, and they claimed that they had made tea but it was more water than tea. There was no sugar because there wasn't enough for everyone so that only the first people who got the tea actually got something, all the rest we just got some water. So this is how it went on for days. One day we would get cheese, the next day the hotdogs, until the second when, for the first time, they made some beans. That's when the Red Cross arrived and that's when we had the hot meal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What effect did this -- the amount of food that you had, what effect did that have on your weight in those 12 days?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all lost weight. We were just provided with enough food not to die, so it was really the minimum that you could really survive on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When were you finally released from Stajicevo camp? What date?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of December around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that the same day that the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did they have a role in your being released that day?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many other people were released with you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Nadas and myself, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why the -- Dr. Nadas who you said was Jewish and you being born in Syria, why were the two of you released?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, on the fourth or fifth day of our arrival at the camp, he told me personally that the Syrian government had contacted the Serbian government in relation to me and that there were talks going on and that I would be certainly be released. Dr. Nadas told him -- about Dr. Nadas, he was told that the Jewish organisation from America requested that he be released. Now, when the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, representatives arrived, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic wanted to show-off. He would say, Well, yes, true, this is a camp. There aren't any sanitary facilities, but we do have doctors. So he called the two of us and then I presented myself. I said what my name was. And then they were wondering how it was that I was there because I was Syrian, and he said that it was an error and they were working on it and they would release him. Then came Dr. Nadas, he also said that he was Jewish, and so the Red Cross then interceded and they intervened and they wanted to work out our release.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure how much time I have left, but with the leave of the Court I'd like permission just to continue for another ten minutes and then I'd be finished with my questioning of Dr. Malla, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Biersay. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Malla, at any time during your detention at the Stajicevo camp, were you ever formally charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during your 12 days there, were any of the other prisoners in the barn with you ever charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe the physical effects of the camp conditions as far as the weight is concerned. What other physical effects stemmed from the conditions in the camp for you personally?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, physical consequences other than the beating that I was exposed to, I don't know what else I could say. I mean, personally I really cannot understand this. There were five of us who were doctors: Dr. Emedi was a Ruthenian; Dr. Nadas was Jewish; Dr. Karnas, Croatian; Dr. Kuljic, a Serb; and I was a Syrian. We were all treated the same way. We were beaten, we were slapped, and I can't really understand that. We stayed there because we wanted to do our job, and for humanitarian reasons we wanted to assist people. Not one of us was a soldier or in any way involved in any of this. We were all treated the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Violence was meted out on us. We weren't new in Vukovar or Borovo. We had all been born there, except me, who had lived there from some ten years earlier. So none of us doctors would be suspicious in any way or suspect in any way as being mercenaries or something. We were just doing humanitarian work and for that we were repaid in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you were released, what happened to your health one week later?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One week after you left the camp, did you have any kind of issues with your health?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A week after I was released, a week after the camp I arrived in Zagreb, and then I had a fit. I couldn't breathe. I was taken to the hospital and I was told that I suffered from very bad bronchitis, through time this turned into an asthma. And it was nonspecific asthma; in other words, it was caused by circumstances. Because I had slept just in a shirt there, there was nothing to cover myself. It was minus 20 degrees outside. There was no heating or anything. And I kept going in and out in order to assist patients, and that probably had an effect on my health. As a result and because of the injuries that I had sustained, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993. For almost two years I treated patients.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: For almost two years I had undergone treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the two years during which you had treatment, what was the treatment for?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I was operated on because the shrapnel had to be taken out, then I had these breathing problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did they manage to remove all the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the three operations I still have some shrapnel fragments, I believe seven fragments or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did those fragments have an effect on metal detectors when you had to go through them?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not anymore. But at first when I went to Zagreb and I travelled by plane, it happened. But not anymore because right now they are very deeply embedded and they are encapsulated. They didn't take them out because it would be dangerous. It would be a bigger threat to take them out rather than leave them where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Malla, you talked about these physical effects. What psychological effects did you notice on yourself and in the other prisoners who were in the camp at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see myself as a doctor, primarily. For 1 00 days of the encirclement of the Borovo settlement, the shelling, the daily shelling, all the people who were killed in Borovo settlement, they were neighbours. They were workers where I worked. They were citizens like I was. I could -- there were many who died that I couldn't help. We had to bury them in the backyards, as it were, of their homes because would he couldn't reach the cemetery. Now, for the last -- at the last month we had to drink rain-water. So you can imagine what kind of both physical and mental effect this would have on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And as far as the stay in the detention in the Stajicevo camp itself, how did prisoners react to being in the camp and being under the conditions that you were in?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't protest. They were regularly beaten, insulted, threatened, and if they tried to protest they would probably be killed. If you allow me, I would like to say something. If the Trial Chamber would allow me, I would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I will have to confer with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Dr. Malla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to this day I cannot understand the behaviour of those people. I cannot understand the way we were treated, at least us, the medical staff. While I was in Borovo Naselje I took care of an old man who was 80 years old. He came to me. He was wounded. I gave him all the medical attention he needed. I fed him for over two and a half months and cared for him, and he got well. Now his family, his son, his nephew, they knew of this and they would not help me. That person was the uncle of Mr. Goran Hadzic. That man was the father of Dr. Mladen Hadzic, who was the minister of health. Everyone knew that I was in a camp. In Belgrade my niece told me, and that -- his niece told me that she was crying and telling them they should help me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Malla, could you repeat the last sentence for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to put me in the camp, was that a thank you for what I had done for their father and their uncle? And both of them -- one of them was the prime minister and the other was the minister of health. I helped their father and I cared for him. For two and a half months I fed him. And they knew me very well. Just -- and they knew where I was, just like Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic knew that I was in a camp. I am not a Croat. I'm a doctor from Syria. I was never involved in politics and I was never interested in politics. That is what hurts. That is the psychological effect. That's the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Nothing further at this time, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Malla. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I am the Defence counsel for Goran Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you this: Yesterday you testified and you told us how many doctors there were in Borovo Naselje, that's on page 3847 of the transcript, where you said that at first there were eight - at least that's what is reflected in the transcript - and that later on there were 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Now, tell us, please, in the former Yugoslavia you lived from 1964; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had occasion to meet a lot of people, not only in Borovo Naselje where you resided, but also in Vukovar and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that, among other things, you worked as a doctor of a sports club which was called -- which is called Sindjelic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was that? Could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from 1983 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, what that means, Sindjelic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. I heard there -- I heard them singing something when there were these celebrations. That's all I know about it. But I know there was a song by that name or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said yesterday that you knew well the late Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain why you had difficulty recalling his first name?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? If you mean that first moment where I couldn't recall his name, well, I was just blocked at that moment, and I did recall it later on and I did mention it. I also -- I could recall the name of his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, among other things -- or, do you know where he worked?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vupik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was involved, that he was a politician.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know him at the time when he was the politician?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I met him, I know that he was -- I met him as the president of this club. As a foreigner I was never involved in politics. All I knew was that he was a engineer and that he worked for Vupik, and I never discussed politics with him or parties, political parties, or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you knew that he was an engineer, do you know what he was an engineer of?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an agronomer or an agronomist. Well, if he worked for Vupik then you know what he must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if you can -- or, let me rephrase that. Can you tell us how long the situation was stable in Croatia, in your assessment? You arrived there in 1964. You remain there to this day. When did this situation begin to destabilise in Croatia, if we could put it that way?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat what I said before. I am a doctor. I did not get involved in politics. I was a foreigner. I could not even vote, nor could I be elected. So I didn't think of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that until weapons were used, you didn't really sense that there was any kind of tension in Vukovar or Borovo Naselje that could turn much worse?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were tensions, not just on the eve of the war, also earlier on. In 1984, 1985, during every celebration at the club, towards the end they would sing nationalist songs. They wouldn't sing Yugoslav songs. They would start singing, "Who is singing, who is lying that Serbia is small?" That's not a Yugoslav song. That's a nationalist song. I knew this, although I was a foreigner, so I was not really bothered by it, but there were tensions. When the HDZ won, the Communists lost power and nationalists came to power on both sides. That's when the tensions began and increased. There were tensions among the politicians. But the people were the ones who suffered, the regular folk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to clarify your answer. So there were tensions when this song was sung at the celebration of the club?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just one song, the Sindjelic song, that was the first time I heard it, but I wasn't bothered by it. They would sing. I have sat there. Maybe I even joined in. I didn't really care about that. This was a celebration. We were celebrating our victory. So there were these things, so I'm sure there was this on the other side, too, that they sang Ustasha songs. However, where I lived, in Borovo Naselje - and that's what I'm talking about - most of my friends were Serbs, and you -- I couldn't choose them, you know. But friends you can choose. You don't choose acquaintances but you do choose friends, and that's what's so painful, that I was betrayed by friends. A judge, Rade Kojic, he was the best friend I had. And also our families were friends. And three days before he went to Borovo Naselje, he spent the night in my house, and later on he never offered to help nor did he ask about me. And for ten years prior to that, we were friends. We shared food. We shared houses. So for them I was an Ustasha and that was a thank you to me. Those were -- that's true friendship?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Let's be precise about one thing. You said that songs were sung at club celebrations. Was that on the club premises?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the club premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The players, at least 11 players, some with wives, some with mothers, the club management, there was my wife, Slavko's wife as well, Milenko who was the president of the hunter's society and his wife. It was a family celebration. We all had our families with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you put this answer within the context of my question, and the question was about the time when tensions started emerging in Croatia, Vukovar and Borovo Selo, would you say that singing among the 30 or 50 people in the club caused the tensions in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That club was just one segment. There was another segment in another village or in the next village, and all of a sudden those small segments amount to a lot, because this -- that was just a circle that I was in. I don't know about the others. I wasn't there. But I suppose the situation was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, this was the only place where you heard that, in that club?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was a doctor in other clubs as well, but that club was a Serb club and the village was a Serb village. The rest of the clubs were different. There was the Borovo cyclist club, the weight lifters Borovo, the karate club Borovo, and their members were from Borovo, and Borovo was the sponsor of all of those teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To my earlier question you answered that certain tensions started emerging after the HDZ won the elections in Croatia. Why would you say that the HDZ's victory caused those tensions?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ was a nationalist party and the Serbs just didn't like that. There were nationalist parties in Serbia as well. And that's how things happened. It was a power struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had a lot of Serb friends. Did they tell you why they were bothered by the HDZ's victory? Why they did not like the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Let me explain in a different way. All of my friends, the Serbs who had been members of the League of Communists, over night transformed from members of the League of Communists into ultranationalists. They no longer sang Yugoslav songs. They started singing nationalist songs all of a sudden over night. I just cannot comprehend that. Either they were false communists or they became false nationalists, because you cannot transform yourself within a day or even seven days into something completely different. For example, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, he was also a member of the League of Communists and he held high positions in the League of Communists. He would not have become president of the executive council or the president of the city board if he hasn't been a communist. And all of a sudden - all of a sudden - he started rooting for the Serbs. He forgot about Yugoslavia. He became a fervent Serb. And as an engineer he started fighting. He had a different agenda, and I did not understand that. How did they travel that journey, from being members of the League of Communists to being nationalists? I apologise. Not only him and not only Serbs. The same thing happened in Croatia. There were Croatian members of the League of Communists who turned coat over night and they became Croatian nationalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn that those people became turncoats over night and that they became nationalists, for example, the Serbs that you knew? What's the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio, television, speeches were delivered. They were actively working on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many of your friends expressed such positions on radio and television?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dokmanovic, for example, did he deliver speeches? Yes. After the fall of Vukovar or the liberation of Vukovar, call it what you want, was he the mayor of Vukovar? Yes, he was. During the communist era he also occupied a very prominent position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Slavko Dokmanovic, who had been a member of the League of Communists and later on that party was renamed into the Party for Democratic Changes under the leadership of Ivica Racan, do you know that that party advocated the stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were communists, I know, yes. But they were a minority in Belgrade and in Zagreb. The HDZ was power in Croatia and another nationalist party was in power in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at the time Dokmanovic was a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was the mayor of Vukovar for a while. Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still in touch with him, I didn't know what was his political affiliation. I've told you, we were friends. If we got together, we talked about the players, the club, the injuries, we had a drink together, we shared a bite. I was never involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you were not involved in politics, but I see that you are privy to a lot of information concerning politics, and you've just shared it with us.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information that I learned subsequently from the radio, television, and newspapers. But while I was there, while I worked there, I was not involved in politics. I did not have the right to be involved in politics. As a foreigner who did not have the Croatian citizenship, I could not be a member of any party. I was not allowed to be involved in politics even if I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you followed political life only through the media?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't get involved in any of the developments that were unfolding there at that time, and I mean the tensions between, for example, those parties, the HDZ on the one side, the League of Communists or the Party for Democratic Changes, as it was later known, the Serbian Democratic Party, and so on and so forth? You didn't get involved in that?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now just something else I would like to hear from you. At the beginning of those conflicts, as it were, did you hear that there were people, that there were Serbs who were killed in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For example in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have the information, you will know that I was a resident in Zagreb and I would come to Borovo only on weekends, on Friday evening to see my wife and children, and on Sunday evening I would return to Zagreb. I was a resident in occupation medicine at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was that? When were you absent from Vukovar, i.e., from Borovo Naselje for that reason?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1988, for three years I was a resident in Zagreb, in Osijek, and I would be at home only on weekends and for summer holidays when I would take my family to the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you did arrive to see your family, you would also attend football games, you would examine the players?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I became a resident I no longer worked for any of the clubs or teams. I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So whatever you have just told us about your contacts with the football team and other athletes stopped in 1988?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was still friends with those people. I could no longer work for them, but I was still friends with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you complete your residency? When did you return to Borovo Naselje or to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 1st of July because I enrolled at the post-graduate studies and I completed at the end of June, and I arrived in Borovo in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps know some of the residents of Borovo, one was Dragan Mijatovic, the other was Stojan Stojanovic? Did you ever hear of them?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps know people from Borovo Naselje whose name -- names were Zdravko Komsic, Mirko Nujic, Stjepan Mackovic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names do ring a certain bell but I can't remember them. First of all, let me explain one thing: I was a doctor. I was a GP in a company that employed 20.000 people. I know many of the names. I know many of the face, but very often I can't put the two together. I can't recall everybody. I know my friends by name, but the others who were my patients, I may recall their names but vaguely or I can't put their names to their faces. They were my patients, they were not my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew Dr. Mladen Hadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From when?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment I started working in Borovo. He was a dermatologist there in Vukovar. I referred my patients to him. I had a lot of patients with skin problems, allergies, I referred my patients to him in those cases, and two or three occasions he came to the company as a visiting doctor, and I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you actually meet Dr. Hadzic? Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived. As soon as I started working. We were not friends, we did not socialise, but we were colleagues and we had contacts through our patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Dr. Hadzic lived? Where he resided?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I would like to ask the witness to clarify when he started working. You said when I started working, "When did you actually meet Dr. Hadzic? Do you remember the year?" When I arrived, when I started working. Is that 1991, July 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 1982. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in 1992 but 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I said. Then one more clarification that I should -- I must find it. Just one moment. When you told us that you -- after you completed your residency, you enrolled at the post-graduate studies that you completed at the end of June. And then you came back to Vukovar around the 1st of July. That would be 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that you met Dr. Hadzic, do you know where he worked?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I referred my patients to him. I'm sure that he worked either in Osijek or in Vukovar. I did not have any contacts with him. I would give my patients referral notes and then they would go to him, and then they brought back his papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you this because I heard that he was the director of all the outpatient clinics in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been a director but he was also a specialist. He was a dermatologist and he saw patients. I don't know. I know that I referred my patients to him, and when I did that I did not send them specifically to him but to a dermatologist, but the findings that I then received were signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, he lived in Tenja?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've told you I don't know. I didn't say that we were friends, that I ever visited him. We were colleagues and I knew of him. I knew about him through my patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you never had any direct contacts with him? You didn't contact him either personally or by phone?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask this is because of the last portion of your testimony where you said that you treated his father and, among other things, you said that he was Goran Hadzic's uncle on the father side.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was told. I was told that by the daughter of Dr. Hadzic after the camp when I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what her name was?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was released from the camp. I went with Dr. Nadas to sleep at his brother's place; his brother, Brane Nadas, who had a company in Belgrade. And on the following day, he took us to his company and he asked me, Well, do you want to call up Zagreb to find out what was going on with your family? And I said, Yes. And there was a young woman working there. She helped me get through the phone lines via Bosnia to Zagreb, and I -- once the conversation -- I finished the conversation, she asked me, Are you Dr. Hicham? And I said, Yes. And then she started to cry and she thanked me, and she said, You saved my grandfather. And then I said, Well, so he made it? Because before the fall of Vukovar, on the 12th or 13th, I believe, he was on his bike biking towards Borovo Selo. He said he could no longer stay there, he couldn't survive, he had no food. And I told him, Old man, don't go. It was dark, there was shooting. And I didn't see him after that. This was the 11th. On the 12th of November he came to the shelter because he heard that I was wounded, so he brought some tobacco, pipe tobacco and cigarettes. He said, Cigarettes for your wife, and the pipe -- the pipe tobacco for you. And then I told him that my wife had been killed. He didn't know that. And every time -- because he would come to the shelter to sleep there, I saw this one night that he wasn't going away - it was already 11.00 - so I asked him, Do you want to sleep here? And he said, No, but I want to talk to you. And then we talked and he said he could no longer take it, that there was nothing to eat, and that he was going to Borovo Selo. He took his bike, and I said, Why don't you wait a little? It will be over soon. And I thought that I had persuaded him. But then I heard from his daughter that he had succeeded, that at the -- on the outskirts of Borovo Selo there was an APC, that they let him through, and he told me at the time that he had a granddaughter and how he had been saved and so on. So this granddaughter thanked me, and then I asked, Well, is he your father? And you can tell him that he could have helped me while I was in the camp, because he knew that I was in the camp and I was a doctor. Now, this daughter, she wasn't working in her line of work. She was helping out with this company, because I know that she had graduated from a nursing school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify. Perhaps you said that, but I didn't quite understand you: Where was this that Dr. Hadzic's daughter was working when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brane Nadas from Vukovar, the brother of Dr. Nadas. Now, he lived in Belgrade, so when we left the camp we went to see him in Belgrade and we spent the night in his house. He had a company there and this woman was working for him in the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see, thank you. Now, you were in close touch with Dr. Hadzic's father. Did he tell you what relationship he had with his son; in other words, with Dr. Mladen Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this: He did not tell me who he was and I did not ask him. He came to see me - I remember this very well - he came early in the morning, he came to the shelter, and he asked me whether I could see him, and I said, Of course I can. The only thing that I saw - this was wartime - this man came, he was dressed in a fine dark blue suit, and it was my opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I apologise. You have answered my question already. There is no need to give us more details about this man.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just want to tell you that I learned who he was -- well, I offered him food. He said he didn't have any food, and I told him, Look, we have a shelter where I am. Do come over because you will be fed every day. So on the first day he did get food. Now, on the second day, the person who was in charge of the shelter, he said, Doctor, don't let this man come anymore. And I said, Why not? He said, Well, do you know who this man was? And then he told me who he was. And one of the cooks complained why we were feeding him while his sons are shooting at us. So I told them, First of all, this person is a patient of mine so he must be given a meal, and I am entitled to one meal a day as your doctor, so give him my meal. Now he -- when he came to see me, he wouldn't even enter the shelter. He would stay outside on the steps and he would eat his food there and he would leave because he was uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me just this - it may be unclear from something you said - you said that he was Goran Hadzic's uncle. Does that mean that their father's are brothers?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Hadzic's daughter told me that Goran was her uncle. Now, what kind of uncle, whether on the father's side or the mother's side, I didn't ask that. She just said that Mr. Goran was her uncle. Now, whether he was a close relative or a removed, once or twice removed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the reason I'm asking this is that even their great, great, great grandfathers weren't brothers, so that's why I'm asking you whether you were told what kind of kin they were and how it was that he could be Goran Hadzic's uncle.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Hadzic's daughter told me that he was her uncle. I didn't ask her about the details and I wasn't really interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you would move to another topic, this would be an appropriate time, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you. Dr. Malla, it's time for our first break. We'll come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber received a Defence request about the Orthodox Easter on the 6th of May, if I'm not mistaken. We heard that OTP has no position on that request. We will grant that request and sit that week on Friday instead of Monday. So that would be 10th of May or the 11th, but that same week instead of sitting Monday we will sit Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malla, would you now take a look at a brief video-clip; that's 4954.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We did not receive the transcript for this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can stop here to provide the interpreters with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We have the transcripts now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We will start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I am Dr. Hicham Malla from Borovo Naselje. I carried my working there during that time of war. One could not think about the time. One had to work or not to work. Shells were not limited to certain time-periods, to eight hours a day, and they were not fired during the working hours only. No one was supposed to work all the time. As long as there were patients -- as long as there were -- when the first convoy arrived with the medical supplies, I received a part of it. After that, I didn't get anything. The rest I received from the guard, military police, people brought it from [indiscernible]. That's how we used medical supplies. I think there is not a single other war with so many violations as it was, because this was a war fought by mortars. In the Second World War, one did not use mortars as much as here. Here, one used shells, howitzers, mortars, and you know what happens when a shell explodes into 3.000 shrapnel pieces. I have been very long in Croatia, and I do not feel any different from any other Croat. I participated in one civil war in Lebanon, and I knew what would happen and how this war would be fought. I said at the health centre in Borovo that if such a war would break out here, and yet none of my colleagues believed me. But when the war started they fled and nobody remained. "It was already in May when I suggested that each shelter should be adapted into a medical facility. I warned then that wounded people would not even be able to cross the street, let alone come to a certain place. They did not believe me. I organised a shelter where I was able to do so, and ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malla, you remember this interview that you gave?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that it is dated 18th of October, 1991. Is that when it happened?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in is the last portion that we discussed here and that we did not have information on before. The portion where you said that you took part in the civil war in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when this was?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1979 through 1981, the end of 1981. I was in Syria with my family, the entire family, and my sister lived in Lebanon. She was married there and lived there. From Damascus it's some 60 kilometres away. I went there to help people because of the war, and then I saw what the fighting looked like. There was street fighting. There were all kinds of militias. Wounded people would die because you couldn't reach the hospital. So I thought if the war broke out, we should have at least a doctor and a nurse in every shelter and that we should do something about it to help out. And this is what I told my director after the 2nd of May. I said that the situation didn't look good, and you probably know what had happened elsewhere. But my director refused. He said, No, if something does happen it will happen, and we'll be there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood from your evidence that you have been in Croatia since 1964.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1979 I left my job in Zagreb. My parents were old at the time. I am their oldest son. I was a doctor. They asked me to come to work in Syria, and I was there until the end of 1981 and then I returned. I couldn't stay there. I returned to Croatia. I started looking for a job, and then for six months I worked in Prijedor. I was looking for a better position. And then in 1982 I landed a job in Vukovar in the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So from 1979 to 1981 you worked in Syria; right?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were you in Lebanon?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, it was when I was living on the border with Lebanon, because that war Lebanon had been going on for 15 years, so I went there, to the front line to help the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, while you worked in Syria were you sent to Lebanon to work there, or did you go there of your own volition?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not sent anywhere. I didn't have to work in Borovo. I was a resident of Zagreb. I interrupted my residency, and I went there to help the people with whom I lived. I was in Zagreb. I was a resident for three years. I did not have to go back to Vukovar. There were a lot of people who were residents in Zagreb, who hailed from Vukovar, and didn't return to Vukovar. I wanted to go where I was most needed. Why should I go there after the war and then have people asking me, Where were you during the war when you were needed the most? I wanted to go there when I was needed the most, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you have told us two different things. While you were in Lebanon were you paid?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of doctors all over the world who are volunteers; for example, Medecins Sans Frontieres. It's humanitarian work that they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of Medecins Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Lebanon, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed with my sister who lived very close to the border. She had a family there. She had a husband who hailed from Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more thing, you have just told us that you interrupted your residency. The way I understood your evidence was that you returned to Vukovar on the 1st of July because you had completed your residency?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I completed my post-graduate studies. As for my residence, I had to complete practical work on the different wards. I completed my residency after the war. I took all of my exams for the post-graduate studies, and that's a normal educational cycle, from autumn to summer. That's why I returned to Vukovar on the 1st of July. And as for my residency, I did everything that was necessary to complete it but I did it after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It arises from your statement that already in the month of May you envisaged what kind of war would be waged in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did that owing to -- strike that. Tell me, how could you know that there would be war in the month of May, and especially such a terrible war?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you know what happened on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo. Wasn't there a massacre over there? Don't you know it? There was a massacre. What else did one need? Twenty MUP members were killed there on the 2nd of May, would you not call that war, or at least a sign that there would be war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You said on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just finish my question. Did you say that 20 MUP members were killed?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard. Two police officers were taken prisoner and the others came to liberate them, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this: How could you know on the 2nd of May? Because I don't see how ordinary people could foresee the outcome, that there would be conflicts and armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you had lived in Borovo Naselje and in Vukovar, you would have known as well. There were barricades around every single village. On every single road, there were roadblocks. There were weapons. It didn't bode well, did it? Could you say that those were tell-tale signs of peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time a lot of political negotiations were going on, although you said that you were not involved in politics, but you followed the media. And I'm sure that you heard that there were talks involving the Serbian side and the Croatian side and all the other factors.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were talks, there were cease-fires, and we heard it on the radio, and at the same time there were shelling going on. One thing was being said on the radio and the other thing was happening on the ground. It was the lords of war who ran the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about shelling but I believe there was no shelling in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't, but you asked me about politicians. This was my example. We heard that there were talks, there were negotiation, but the situation on the ground was completely different. What I'm saying is not everything you heard on the radio and on television could be trusted. No everything materialised the way it was portrayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask the Trial Chamber to admit this video into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 4954.1 shall be assigned Exhibit D35. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about some citizens of Borovo Selo of Serbian ethnicity and some others who were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D249. I'm interested in the second page of the document. We don't have a B/C/S translation. This is a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at chapter 1 on page 2 about intentional killings of civilians, and look at Roman I and 1-001. It says here briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that on the 4th of July, 1991, in Borovo Naselje, Dragan Mijatovic, Stojan Stojanovic, and some other people were killed. They were Serbs, they were not identified, and there is a list of suspects underneath. Did you hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the following page, 1-008 is the chapter that I would like to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, there is a reference to the killing of a Serb from Borovo Naselje whose name was Ilija Lozancic. Again there is a list of suspects. Did you hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. I'm not sure where Mr. Zivanovic is going with this. So far he's read into the record two blocks from this document. The witness, even before, said that he'd not heard of these people. The question and the documents were still put to him, so at this time I'd object. If Mr. Zivanovic has questions for the witness, he should ask him without showing him the document, essentially reading it into the record only to have the witness say that he's never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask to -- for this document to be admitted. I just confronted the witness with this, with the content of this document, and I would like to give the source of my information about this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm happy to find the transcript cite, but I believe the witness was asked about whether or not he knew about crimes against Serbs, and he said no at that time. I will try to find the transcript page. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but that's what I understood, and I think now to read these portions of the document into the record is prejudicial and unreliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if you want to know whether the witness knows anything about particular incidents, I think it would be appropriate to ask the witness directly without showing him this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the name Milan Djukic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know him at all? He was from Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Cedo Jovic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A waiter whose family name was Pantic?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Siladzin?

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: If you showed me their photos, maybe I would remember them, but I don't remember their names. And when all of these happened, I was not there. I was there on the 2nd of May because of the bank holiday, then I returned to Zagreb to complete my post-graduate studies. So if all those things happened, and I suppose that they did, how would I have been in a position to know? I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have all the people whose names I mentioned to you were alive on the 2nd of May, which is one thing; and second of all, I'm asking you about these people because you said that you knew a lot of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am a doctor. Just bear with me for a moment. In the Borovo company, over 70 per cent employees were Serbs, and they were all my patients. I -- I knew them, but I could not remember. I cannot remember their names. But they will know me, they will know me as their doctor. As for the document that you are showing me, I can be almost sure that I knew them all. There are very few people from Borovo Selo, Trpinja, Vukovar, who didn't work in the company or their families did not work in the companies. But there were 20.000 of them. How do you expect me to remember all of their names 22 years after the events? You can ask me about what I did, what I experienced, but as to what happened before or what happened after or what happened while I wasn't there, how am I supposed to know all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am restricting my questions to some persons. I am asking you whether you know them, whether you knew them. I am not asking you whether you know that -- about any harm that happened to them.

utterances.speaker: HICHAM MALLA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you, I probably know 90 per cent of them because I was their doctor. I lived with them for so many years, but I can't really remember all of their names, or I can't put any faces to the names. I am not a computer. I cannot promptly recall their names and their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
